T1A01: Part 97.1 lists five purposes for amateur radio; advancing technical and communication skills is explicitly one of them, reflecting the service's educational mission.
T1A02: The FCC is the U.S. federal agency empowered to write and enforce Part 97, which governs all amateur radio operation in the country.
T1A03: FCC rules encourage phonetic alphabets during voice calls to reduce misunderstanding of letters — it's a best practice, not a requirement.
T1A04: After exam credit is filed, the FCC sends you an email with a link to download your official license grant from the ULS system.
T1A05: The ULS database entry is the legal proof of license; a printed copy is convenient but the database record is what counts under Part 97.
T1A06: Part 97.203(d) reserves 28.200–28.300 MHz on 10 meters specifically for automatically controlled propagation beacons, making that the segment to monitor for beacon signals.
T1A07: Part 97 draws the line at 50 km altitude; above that threshold an amateur station is classified as a space station regardless of orbit type.
T1A08: Frequency coordinators are volunteers chosen by the local amateur community to recommend channels for repeater and auxiliary stations to minimize interference.
T1A09: Operators of eligible repeater and auxiliary stations in a local or regional area collectively choose who serves as their frequency coordinator — a peer-selected role.
T1A10: RACES links amateur radio to civil emergency management, so operators must hold both an FCC license and active enrollment in a recognized civil defense organization.
T1A11: Deliberately disrupting another station's communication is explicitly forbidden by Part 97; the word willful distinguishes intentional jamming from accidental interference.
T1B01: On HF, Technicians earn phone privileges only in the 28.300–28.500 MHz slice of 10 meters; all other HF phone segments require General class or higher.
T1B02: The ISS communicates on VHF frequencies that fall within the Technician band allocation, so any Technician or higher licensee may legally make contact.
T1B03: The 6-meter band spans 50–54 MHz; 52.525 MHz falls within that range and is the national FM simplex calling frequency for the band.
T1B04: The 2-meter band covers 144–148 MHz; 146.52 MHz is the national FM simplex calling frequency and a standard landmark for new Technicians.
T1B05: Technicians have digital privileges on portions of several HF bands (80, 40, 15, and 10 meters) as well as all VHF/UHF bands, so all listed choices apply.
T1B06: On HF, Technicians receive phone privileges only in 28.300–28.500 MHz on 10 meters; other HF bands restrict Technicians to CW and digital modes only.
T1B07: The bottom 100 kHz of both 6 meters and 2 meters are reserved exclusively for CW, preserving a quiet Morse-only segment in each band.
T1B08: When amateur radio is secondary in a band segment, amateurs must not interfere with primary users and must accept interference from them — they cannot complain or claim priority.
T1B09: Calibration drift, sideband splatter, and filter roll-off can each independently push a signal outside the band edge, so all of those reasons apply simultaneously.
T1B10: FCC Part 97.305(c) authorizes SSB phone in designated segments across every amateur band above 50 MHz, so there is always at least one SSB-permitted segment regardless of which specific band you're on.
T1B11: FCC Part 97.313 caps Technician power on HF privileges at 200 W PEP—much lower than the 1500 W general limit—reflecting the narrower HF access Technicians receive.
T1B12: Above 30 MHz, Technicians share the same 1500 W PEP ceiling as General and Extra class operators; the lower 200 W limit applies only to their restricted HF segments below 30 MHz.
T1C01: The FCC eliminated the Novice and Advanced license classes and no longer issues new ones; only Technician, General, and Amateur Extra are available to new applicants today.
T1C02: FCC Part 97.19 lets any licensed amateur—regardless of class—apply for a specific available call sign through the vanity program; no special tier or seniority is required.
T1C03: Part 97.117 limits international amateur contacts to hobby-related exchanges and personal conversation, keeping it non-commercial and consistent with the service's communication and goodwill purposes.
T1C04: FCC Part 97.23 requires a current, working email address in your license record; if the FCC can't reach you with official notices, it can revoke or suspend your license.
T1C05: Group D call signs follow a 2-letter prefix, one digit, three-letter suffix (2x3) format. KF1XXX matches exactly; the other options use patterns not assigned to Group D Technicians.
T1C06: Part 97.5(a)(2) allows a US-licensed amateur to operate from a US-documented vessel in international waters as long as the ship's master grants permission.
T1C07: FCC rules allow you to file for renewal starting 90 days before your license expires, giving you a window to renew without any lapse in authorization.
T1C08: FCC grants amateur radio licenses with a standard 10-year term; you must renew before expiration to maintain uninterrupted operating authority.
T1C09: After an amateur license expires, Part 97.21 provides a two-year grace period to renew without retesting—but transmitting is prohibited during that entire grace period.
T1C10: Your authorization to transmit begins the moment your grant appears in the FCC's Universal Licensing System database; a CSCE from your exam session is not sufficient to operate.
T1C11: An expired license conveys no operating authority, even within the two-year grace period. You must complete the renewal and have a valid grant before transmitting again.
T1D01: If a country's government notifies the ITU that it objects to amateur communications from other nations, FCC Part 97 prohibits US stations from contacting amateurs in that country.
T1D02: Amateur radio is a two-way communication service. Transmitting to a general, anonymous audience—broadcasting—is prohibited because it serves no legitimate amateur communication or training purpose.
T1D03: Encryption is generally banned on amateur radio to keep communications open to monitoring. The narrow exception permits encoded control signals sent to satellites or remotely piloted model craft.
T1D04: Music is normally prohibited on amateur frequencies. The sole exception covers incidental music contained in authorized retransmissions of manned spacecraft communications, such as NASA crew transmissions.
T1D05: You may mention personal amateur gear you're selling, but only occasionally. Running any kind of regular swap-meet or commercial trading operation over amateur frequencies violates Part 97.113.
T1D06: Part 97.113(a)(4) contains a flat prohibition—no exceptions—against indecent or obscene language on any amateur frequency. The rule does not provide a context or intent-based exemption.
T1D07: An auxiliary station carries one-way linking signals, typically routing audio from a remote receiver back to a repeater's main transmitter. FCC Part 97 defines this specific relay role as an auxiliary station.
T1D08: Part 97 broadly prohibits paid amateur operation but carves out an explicit exception when the communication is part of formal classroom instruction at an educational institution.
T1D09: Supporting broadcast or news production is normally barred, but an emergency exception applies when human life or property is directly threatened and no alternative communication means exists.
T1D10: Amateur radio is a two-way communications service; the FCC defines broadcasting as one-way transmissions intended for the general public, a purpose incompatible with the amateur service's mission.
T1D11: Part 97.215 specifically exempts model-craft control signals from the identification requirement because they are brief, one-way command pulses rather than conventional amateur communications.
T1D12: Part 97 requires every on-air transmission, including informal tests, to be identified with the station's call sign so other operators can determine who is transmitting.
T1E01: Part 97.7 is unconditional: a licensed control operator must be responsible for every transmission. No circumstance — not automation, not emergencies — removes that requirement.
T1E02: Satellite access is tied to uplink frequency privileges; any amateur whose license class authorizes operation on that uplink band may use the satellite regardless of other band differences.
T1E03: Part 97.103(b) assigns this duty to the station licensee, who bears ultimate accountability for the station and must formally designate who serves as control operator.
T1E04: Because the control operator is responsible for transmissions, the station's frequency privileges are capped at whatever that operator's license class authorizes, not the licensee's class.
T1E05: The control point is the physical location where the operator actively exercises control — it may be at the transmitter site or somewhere entirely remote.
T1E06: License class determines frequency privileges absolutely; a Technician simply has no authorization for Extra-class-only segments, and no arrangement with another operator can grant that access.
T1E07: Part 97.103(a) holds both accountable: the licensee is responsible for the station itself, and the control operator is jointly responsible for each transmission made.
T1E08: Repeaters retransmit without a human deciding each transmission, satisfying the FCC definition of automatic control — the station operates under programmed or event-driven logic rather than direct human action.
T1E09: Part 97.109(c) places no restriction on which stations may be remotely controlled; any amateur station qualifies as long as a licensed control operator remains responsible.
T1E10: Operating a transmitter via the internet puts the operator at a separate location from the radio, matching the FCC's definition of remote control through a control link.
T1E11: The control operator is the licensed amateur who assumes FCC responsibility for the station's transmissions, ensuring all on-air activity complies with Part 97 rules.
T1F01: Part 97.103(c) requires licensees to make their station and records immediately available upon request; the FCC's inspection authority is unconditional and does not require advance notice.
T1F02: Tactical identifiers are operationally useful but have no legal standing; Part 97 still requires you to transmit your FCC-assigned call sign at least every 10 minutes and at sign-off.
T1F03: Part 97.119(a) sets the identification interval at 10 minutes during a contact plus a final identification when the communication ends, regardless of how long the exchange lasts.
T1F04: FCC Part 97 requires phone stations to identify in English so other operators and the public can understand the call sign, even if the conversation itself is in another language.
T1F05: Part 97 allows a phone station to identify either by speaking the call sign or by sending it in Morse code, giving flexibility while still satisfying the ID requirement.
T1F06: The rules permit any descriptive self-assigned indicator—such as mobile, portable, or a location suffix—so all listed examples are valid additions to a transmitted call sign.
T1F07: The FCC only permits an unlicensed person to communicate through your station to a foreign amateur when a bilateral third-party traffic agreement exists between the US and that country.
T1F08: Third-party communications occur when a licensed control operator transmits a message on behalf of someone else—a person who is not themselves a licensed amateur—to another amateur station.
T1F09: A repeater receives a signal and simultaneously retransmits it on a different frequency, extending coverage for stations that could not otherwise reach each other directly.
T1F10: FCC rules hold the originating station's control operator responsible for what is transmitted; the repeater trustee is not liable for content the repeater inadvertently passes along.
T1F11: FCC Part 97 sets a hard floor of four members for any club seeking a club station license grant.
T2A01: A standard 600 kHz split between a repeater's receive and transmit frequencies lets radios across the country use the same pre-programmed offset on the 2-meter band.
T2A02: 146.520 MHz is the nationally coordinated FM simplex calling frequency where hams listen and announce availability before moving to a working channel.
T2A03: The 70-centimeter band uses a ±5 MHz repeater offset—much wider than 2 meters—because the band itself is far wider and higher-frequency circuits tolerate the larger split.
T2A04: Standard courtesy is to address the other station's call sign first so they know they're being called, then give your own call sign for identification.
T2A05: Giving the CQ station's call sign confirms you heard them, and immediately following with your own call sign tells them who is answering.
T2A06: CQ is the standard solicitation for any contact; repeating it with your call sign and then pausing gives nearby stations time to hear you and respond.
T2A07: A repeater transmits on a different frequency than it receives, and the repeater offset is simply the numerical difference between those two frequencies.
T2A08: CQ is a traditional procedural signal that means you are calling any station and welcoming a reply from any licensed amateur who hears you.
T2A09: Saying your call sign followed by the word listening is the conventional shorthand to signal you are on frequency and open to a contact without issuing a full CQ call.
T2A10: Band plans are voluntary, community-developed guidelines that coordinate how amateurs use different modes and activities within a band, supplementing but not replacing FCC allocations.
T2A11: Simplex operation means both stations use the identical frequency to both transmit and receive, unlike a repeater setup where input and output frequencies differ.
T2B01: Activating reverse temporarily tunes your radio to the repeater's input frequency so you can hear the station transmitting to the repeater rather than the repeater's output.
T2B02: A sub-audible tone transmitted below the voice range that unlocks a receiver's squelch only when the matching tone is detected, keeping the channel quiet from unwanted signals.
T2B03: Multiple repeaters are interconnected so any signal received by one is simultaneously retransmitted by all, greatly extending the network's effective coverage area.
T2B04: Wrong offset, missing CTCSS tone, incorrect access code, or insufficient signal strength can each prevent your transmission from activating a repeater even when you can hear its output.
T2B05: Speaking too loudly causes over-deviation, pushing the FM signal beyond its designed bandwidth; the receiver's limiting circuits then clip the excess, producing audio dropout at loud peaks.
T2B06: DTMF encodes commands as pairs of simultaneous audio tones — the same system used on telephone keypads — letting operators send control signals to repeaters or autopatches.
T2B07: Digital repeaters route traffic by group ID; you must program the correct talkgroup ID into your radio so the system recognizes and routes your transmissions to the intended group.
T2B08: Amateur frequencies are shared and unowned, so stations causing mutual interference are expected to negotiate courteously — one may move, take turns, or agree on another arrangement.
T2B09: Simplex lets two nearby stations communicate directly on one frequency without keying a repeater, preserving repeater capacity for operators who actually need the extended range.
T2B10: QRM is the Q-code for interference from other radio stations; sending it tells your contact that other transmissions are disrupting your ability to copy their signal.
T2B11: QSY is the Q-code for changing operating frequency; a station sending QSY is either announcing it is moving or asking the other station to shift to a specified frequency.
T2B12: A DMR color code is a numeric identifier (0–15) that must match between your radio and the repeater, preventing unintended access from other radios sharing the same channel.
T2B13: Squelch silences the receiver's audio when no signal is present, eliminating the constant static you would otherwise hear between transmissions.
T2B14: A DMR talkgroup is a virtual group ID that routes audio only to radios subscribed to that group, preventing unrelated conversations on the same repeater from interrupting each other.
T2C01: Part 97 governs all amateur station operation without exception; no emergency, authority, or circumstance suspends these rules for a licensed amateur.
T2C02: The Net Control Station opens the net on schedule, solicits check-ins, and directs who communicates with whom, keeping all traffic orderly and efficient.
T2C03: The NATO phonetic alphabet assigns a distinct spoken word to each letter, eliminating confusion between similar-sounding letters like B and D when copying over a noisy signal.
T2C04: RACES is a Part 97 framework authorizing licensed amateurs to provide communications support to civil defense authorities during officially declared local, state, or national emergencies.
T2C05: In net operation, traffic means formal structured messages — similar to written letters — relayed between stations in a defined format, distinct from informal conversation.
T2C06: ARES is a voluntary ARRL program where licensed hams pre-register their skills and equipment to serve as a trained emergency communications resource during disasters and public-service events.
T2C07: The Net Control Station manages all transmissions to prevent confusion; unless you have a genuine emergency, wait to be recognized before transmitting so the net stays orderly.
T2C08: Winlink routes amateur radio email using callsign-based addresses like W1ABC@winlink.org, letting operators exchange messages over radio when the internet is unavailable.
T2C09: FCC rules normally confine operators to their licensed frequency privileges, but allow exceeding them when there is an immediate threat to human life or property—a narrow emergency exception.
T2C10: The preamble carries administrative details such as message number, precedence, originating station, and date so traffic handlers can route and track a message through the relay network.
T2C11: Before sending, the originator counts the words in the message body and records that number as the check, allowing the receiving station to verify nothing was lost in transit.
T2C12: RACES operates under civil defense authority, so members must be formally certified by a civil defense agency before they can participate in emergency activations.
T3A01: VHF wavelengths are short enough that moving a few feet changes whether reflected copies of the signal arrive in phase and reinforce, or out of phase and cancel.
T3A02: Leaves and stems contain water, which absorbs UHF and microwave energy. The loss is small for strong signals but significant for weak ones trying to penetrate dense foliage.
T3A03: The weak-signal VHF/UHF community standardized on horizontal polarization for CW and SSB, so both ends of a long-distance link share the same orientation and avoid polarization mismatch loss.
T3A04: Maximum signal transfer requires matching polarization. When one antenna is vertical and the other horizontal, the mismatch can reduce received signal strength by 20 dB or more.
T3A05: VHF/UHF signals reflect off buildings and hillsides similarly to light off a mirror. Aiming your beam at a nearby reflective surface can bounce your signal around an obstruction.
T3A06: As a mobile antenna moves, multipath signals rapidly shift between reinforcing and canceling, producing fast flutter that sounds like a stick dragged across a picket fence.
T3A07: Rain and snow droplets scatter and absorb microwave energy because their size is comparable to the wavelength, noticeably reducing signal range during precipitation.
T3A08: Ionospheric irregularities produce multiple paths of different lengths and phase delays. As those paths shift randomly, the arriving signals combine differently from moment to moment, causing irregular fading.
T3A09: The ionosphere rotates signal polarization through Faraday rotation, producing elliptical polarization at the receiver. Because both orientations are present, either a vertical or horizontal antenna can receive the signal.
T3A10: Copies of the signal arriving via different path lengths reach the receiver at slightly different times, smearing one symbol into the next and raising bit error rates.
T3A11: The ionosphere is a layer of solar-ionized particles 50–600 km above Earth. At HF frequencies it refracts radio waves back toward the surface, enabling long-distance communication.
T3A12: At 10 and 6 meters the wavelength is far larger than a rain droplet or fog particle, so absorption and scattering are negligible and propagation is essentially unaffected.
T3B01: In an electromagnetic wave the electric and magnetic fields oscillate at right angles to each other and both are perpendicular to the direction of travel.
T3B02: Polarization is defined by the direction the electric field oscillates as the wave travels. A vertical electric field means vertical polarization; a horizontal field means horizontal polarization.
T3B03: Radio waves consist of an electric field and a magnetic field oscillating in phase, perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation.
T3B04: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves, identical to visible light but at different frequencies. All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed — the speed of light — through the vacuum of free space.
T3B05: Since all radio waves travel at the same fixed speed, higher frequency means more cycles per second, so each cycle must be physically shorter — wavelength shrinks as frequency rises.
T3B06: Radio waves travel at ~300 million m/s, so dividing that by frequency in MHz directly yields wavelength in meters. This is just the wave equation speed = frequency × wavelength rearranged.
T3B07: Bands are commonly named by their approximate wavelength — '2 meters,' '70 centimeters' — because the size gives an intuitive feel for antenna dimensions and propagation behavior alongside the frequency.
T3B08: VHF stands for Very High Frequency and occupies exactly one frequency decade from 30 to 300 MHz, sitting above HF shortwave but below UHF.
T3B09: UHF (Ultra High Frequency) covers 300 to 3000 MHz — the next decade above VHF, home to the 70 cm amateur band and many consumer wireless devices.
T3B10: HF (High Frequency) spans 3 to 30 MHz and includes the classic shortwave frequencies used worldwide for long-distance ionospheric skip propagation.
T3B11: The speed of light in free space is approximately 3 × 10^8 meters per second, or 300,000,000 m/s — the universal speed constant for all electromagnetic waves.
T3B12: All electromagnetic waves, regardless of frequency, travel at exactly the same speed in free space. Frequency affects wavelength and photon energy, but not propagation speed.
T3C01: UHF travels mostly in straight lines and is too high in frequency for ionospheric reflection, so signals reach only the line-of-sight horizon and cannot bend around Earth's curvature.
T3C02: HF frequencies reflect off the ionosphere, bouncing signals across continents. VHF and higher frequencies generally pass straight through the ionosphere into space rather than returning to Earth.
T3C03: The aurora is a turbulent, constantly shifting ionized curtain. Signals bouncing off it are Doppler-shifted and scattered, producing a characteristic raspy, distorted sound on received audio.
T3C04: Sporadic E is sudden, dense ionization in the E layer that unpredictably reflects VHF signals hundreds of miles, causing strong signals to appear from well beyond the normal horizon.
T3C05: When radio waves strike the sharp edge of a ridge or building, some energy bends around it — allowing signals to reach receivers in the geometric shadow behind the obstruction.
T3C06: Temperature inversions create a refractive atmospheric duct that traps VHF/UHF waves and guides them along Earth's surface far beyond the normal line-of-sight horizon, regularly enabling 300-mile paths.
T3C07: Meteor trails briefly ionize the atmosphere at altitudes that reflect the 6-meter wavelength well, and 6 meters provides enough bandwidth to exploit the short-duration scatter bursts meteors produce.
T3C08: When a warm air mass sits above cooler air, the sharp temperature boundary refracts radio waves downward, trapping them in an atmospheric duct that guides signals far beyond normal range.
T3C09: The F region is energized by sunlight and most ionized during daylight hours; high sunspot activity boosts ionization enough to reflect 10-meter signals over great distances from dawn to shortly after sunset.
T3C10: During sunspot peaks, intense solar radiation raises F region ionization high enough to reflect 6 and 10 meter signals back to Earth — a feat rarely possible during solar minimum.
T3C11: Earth's lower atmosphere acts as a weak refractive medium, bending radio waves slightly around the planet's curvature and pushing the effective radio horizon a bit farther than what eyes can see.
T4A01: A 50-watt mobile radio typically draws about 10-12 amps from a 12V vehicle electrical system; 13.8V is the standard automotive voltage and 12A provides enough headroom for that power output.
T4A02: SWR meters are frequency-sensitive and have power ratings, so a meter calibrated for the wrong band or underrated for your power level will give inaccurate or unsafe readings.
T4A03: Short, heavy-gauge wire has lower resistance, which minimizes the voltage drop (V=IR) during high-current transmit bursts and keeps the radio performing at full power.
T4A04: FT8 is a computer-decoded digital mode; the radio receives audio that the software decodes, and the software generates audio that the radio transmits, so the two devices exchange audio signals.
T4A05: Placing the meter between transmitter and antenna measures actual power delivered to the feed line, where forward and reflected power can both be accurately captured.
T4A06: The computer needs to hear the received signal (receive audio), send encoded tones to the transmitter (transmit audio), and trigger the PTT line (keying) to switch the radio into transmit mode.
T4A07: The computer's line-in jack captures the audio from the transceiver's speaker output so the software can decode received signals.
T4A08: Flat copper strap has a large surface area relative to its cross-section, which greatly reduces RF impedance (skin effect) compared to round wire of the same DC resistance.
T4A09: Ampere-hours divided by average current draw gives hours of runtime; this is Ohm's law applied to battery capacity.
T4A10: A hotspot acts as a personal RF gateway, linking a nearby handheld radio to internet-based digital voice networks like DMR, D-STAR, or System Fusion.
T4A11: Connecting the negative return directly to the battery chassis ground avoids voltage drops and noise from shared vehicle wiring, giving the radio a clean, low-impedance ground reference.
T4A12: An electronic keyer accepts paddle input and automatically generates properly timed dots and dashes, making it easier to send Morse code accurately at higher speeds.
T4B01: Too much microphone gain overdrives the transmitter's audio stages, causing the signal to clip and splatter, which distorts the audio and can interfere with adjacent frequencies.
T4B02: Most transceivers allow frequency entry via a numeric keypad for direct input or a VFO (Variable Frequency Oscillator) knob for tuning incrementally.
T4B03: Squelch mutes the receiver when no signal is present; turning the threshold down until audio is always open ensures even a weak signal above the noise floor will be heard.
T4B04: FM demodulation relies on detecting frequency deviation centered on the correct carrier; even slight offset shifts the demodulation reference, producing audio distortion.
T4B05: The scanner automatically steps through stored or sequential frequencies, pausing when it detects a signal so the operator can monitor activity across multiple channels.
T4B06: RIT (Receiver Incremental Tuning) or Clarifier shifts only the receive frequency slightly, correcting a pitch mismatch without changing your transmit frequency.
T4B07: A code plug is a configuration file programmed into a DMR radio containing frequencies, color codes, timeslots, and talkgroup assignments needed to use specific repeaters and networks.
T4B08: A narrower filter rejects more out-of-band noise and interference, while a wider filter suits broader modes; matching bandwidth to the mode improves readability.
T4B09: DMR organizes users into talk groups; you join a specific group by entering its numeric ID, which tells the repeater or network to route your transmission only to that group's members.
T4B10: SSB voice occupies roughly 2400 Hz of bandwidth; a filter matched to that width passes the full signal while rejecting noise outside it, maximizing signal-to-noise ratio.
T4B11: D-STAR embeds your call sign in each transmission's digital header so the network can route, log, and identify you. The radio won't key up without a valid call sign programmed.
T5A01: The ampere (amp) is the SI unit measuring the rate of electron flow past a point in a circuit — analogous to gallons per minute in a water pipe.
T5A02: The watt is the SI unit of power, representing how fast electrical energy is consumed or produced (joules per second).
T5A03: Current is the term for electrons moving through a conductor, driven by a voltage difference between two points in the circuit.
T5A04: Frequency describes how many complete cycles an AC waveform completes each second, measured in hertz.
T5A05: Voltage is the electrical potential difference (pressure) between two points; without that difference, electrons have no reason to move and no current flows.
T5A06: Hertz (Hz) is the SI unit of frequency, equal to one cycle per second.
T5A07: Metals have a loosely bound outer electron shell, leaving many electrons free to drift and carry charge when a voltage is applied.
T5A08: Glass has tightly bound electrons with no free carriers, so it resists current flow and makes an effective insulator.
T5A09: In AC, voltage polarity reverses periodically, so current flows in one direction then the opposite, completing a full cycle each period.
T5A10: Power is the rate of energy use — how quickly a device converts electrical energy into heat, light, or work.
T5A11: Resistance opposes electron flow regardless of whether the current is DC, AC, or any other type — it's a property of the material, not the current's direction.
T5B01: Milli- means one-thousandth, so 1 ampere equals 1000 milliamperes; 1.5 A × 1000 = 1500 mA.
T5B02: Kilo- means 1000, so 1500 kHz = 1,500,000 Hz (1.5 MHz).
T5B03: Kilo- means one thousand, so one kilovolt equals 1000 volts.
T5B04: Micro- means one-millionth (10⁻⁶), so one microvolt is 0.000001 volts.
T5B05: Milli- means one-thousandth, so 500 milliwatts = 500/1000 = 0.5 watts.
T5B06: 3000 milliamperes ÷ 1000 = 3 amperes, since there are 1000 milliamperes per ampere.
T5B07: MHz and kHz differ by a factor of 1000; 3.525 MHz multiplied by 1000 equals 3525 kHz.
T5B08: Pico is 10^-12 and micro is 10^-6, so one microfarad contains exactly 1,000,000 picofarads.
T5B09: Every time power doubles it increases by 3 dB; 5 watts to 10 watts is exactly a doubling.
T5B10: Every halving of power equals -3 dB; 12 to 3 watts divides by 4 (two halvings), giving -6 dB.
T5B11: A tenfold power increase always equals 10 dB; 200 is exactly 10 times 20.
T5B12: kHz and MHz differ by 1000; dividing 28400 kHz by 1000 gives 28.400 MHz.
T5B13: MHz and GHz differ by 1000; dividing 2425 MHz by 1000 gives 2.425 GHz.
T5C01: Capacitance describes how well a component can store electrical energy in the electric field between its conductive plates.
T5C02: The farad measures capacitance; a one-farad capacitor stores one coulomb of charge when one volt is applied.
T5C03: Inductance describes a coil's ability to store energy in the magnetic field generated by current flowing through it.
T5C04: The henry is the unit of inductance; a one-henry inductor produces one volt when current changes at one amp per second.
T5C05: Impedance is the AC equivalent of resistance, measured in ohms; it combines resistive and reactive opposition to current flow.
T5C06: kHz uses lowercase k (SI convention for kilo) plus Hz; it represents kilohertz, or 1000 cycles per second.
T5C07: MHz uses uppercase M (SI convention for mega) plus Hz; it represents megahertz, or one million cycles per second.
T5C08: Watt's Law states power equals current times voltage; this P = I x E formula applies to all DC power calculations.
T5C09: Using P = I x E: 10 amperes times 13.8 volts equals 138 watts.
T5C10: Using P = I x E: 2.5 amperes times 12 volts equals 30 watts.
T5C11: Rearranging P = I x E gives I = P divided by E; 120 watts divided by 12 volts equals 10 amperes.
T5C12: Impedance is the total opposition to AC current flow, combining resistance and reactance into a single value measured in ohms.
T5D01: Ohm's Law states current equals voltage divided by resistance; this I = E/R formula is the foundation of circuit analysis.
T5D02: Ohm's Law states that voltage equals current multiplied by resistance. This formula, E = I × R, lets you find any one of the three values if the other two are known.
T5D03: Rearranging Ohm's Law to solve for resistance gives R = E / I. Divide the applied voltage by the measured current to find how much the circuit resists current flow.
T5D04: Using R = E / I: 90 volts divided by 3 amperes equals 30 ohms. Ohm's Law directly links these three quantities.
T5D05: R = E / I: 12 volts divided by 1.5 amperes equals 8 ohms. Higher resistance means less current flows for the same voltage.
T5D06: R = E / I: 12 volts divided by 4 amperes equals 3 ohms. A lower resistance allows more current to flow from the same source.
T5D07: I = E / R: 120 volts divided by 80 ohms equals 1.5 amperes. Greater resistance limits how much current the voltage can push through the circuit.
T5D08: I = E / R: 200 volts divided by 100 ohms equals 2 amperes. Doubling the voltage across the same resistor doubles the current.
T5D09: I = E / R: 240 volts divided by 24 ohms equals 10 amperes. A small resistance with high voltage produces a large current.
T5D10: E = I × R: 0.5 amperes times 2 ohms equals 1 volt. Even a small current through a small resistance produces a measurable voltage drop.
T5D11: E = I × R: 1 ampere times 10 ohms equals 10 volts. The voltage drop across a resistor is proportional to both current and resistance.
T5D12: E = I × R: 2 amperes times 10 ohms equals 20 volts. Doubling the current through the same resistor doubles the voltage across it.
T5D13: In a series circuit, all components share a single current path, so the same current must flow through every component. There is no alternate route for electrons to take.
T5D14: In a parallel circuit, each component connects directly across the same two nodes, so all components see the identical voltage regardless of their individual resistance.
T6A01: A resistor is specifically designed to impede electron flow by converting electrical energy to heat. Its resistance value, measured in ohms, determines how much it limits current.
T6A02: A potentiometer is a variable resistor with a sliding or rotating wiper that taps off a fraction of the total resistance, making it ideal for smooth volume adjustment.
T6A03: Turning a potentiometer's shaft moves a wiper along a resistive element, varying the resistance seen by the circuit between zero and the component's maximum rated value.
T6A04: A capacitor stores energy in the electric field between two charged conductors separated by an insulator. It can release that stored energy back into the circuit.
T6A05: A capacitor is built from two conductive plates (or foil layers) with a non-conducting dielectric material between them. The insulating gap allows an electric field to build up and store charge.
T6A06: When current flows through an inductor, it creates a surrounding magnetic field that stores energy. That energy is released back as current when the field collapses.
T6A07: Winding wire into a coil concentrates the magnetic field produced by current flow, greatly increasing the inductance. More turns and a ferromagnetic core increase the effect further.
T6A08: SPDT stands for Single-Pole Double-Throw — one input line connects to either of two output lines, like a railroad switch directing one track to one of two destinations.
T6A09: A single-pole single-throw switch has one input and one output and simply opens or closes a single circuit path — the most basic switch type.
T6A10: Lithium-ion, lead-acid, and nickel-metal hydride can all accept a charging current to restore their chemical energy, making all three rechargeable.
T6A11: Carbon-zinc cells (standard dry cells) undergo irreversible chemical reactions during discharge; attempting to recharge them can cause leakage or rupture.
T6B01: Forward voltage drop varies by semiconductor material — silicon drops about 0.7 V, while Schottky and germanium diodes drop significantly less.
T6B02: A diode's P-N junction creates a one-way gate: it conducts when forward-biased but blocks reverse current, acting like an electrical check valve.
T6B03: A small base or gate signal controls a much larger collector/drain current, so a transistor can switch a circuit on or off electronically.
T6B04: A bipolar junction transistor (BJT) has emitter, base, and collector regions — three alternating layers of P and N semiconductor material.
T6B05: A field-effect transistor uses an electric field at the gate to control current flow between the source and drain terminals.
T6B06: A stripe or band printed near one end marks the cathode (negative terminal), indicating which direction current can flow through the diode.
T6B07: When forward current pushes electrons across the P-N junction, electrons drop to a lower energy state and release that energy as photons of light.
T6B08: FET is simply the abbreviation for Field Effect Transistor, the transistor family that uses an electric field rather than base current for control.
T6B09: The two terminals of a diode are the anode (positive side, current enters) and cathode (negative side, current exits) — terms borrowed from vacuum tube technology.
T6B10: A transistor amplifies by using a small input signal to control a larger current from a power supply, delivering more power out than in.
T6B11: Gain can be expressed as a voltage ratio, a current ratio, or a power ratio — all describe how much an amplifier multiplies the input signal.
T6B12: A BJT has three terminals: the emitter (current source/sink), the base (control input), and the collector (output terminal that handles the larger current).
T6C01: A schematic uses standardized symbols to represent components and lines to show connections, giving technicians a universal map of circuit operation.
T6C02: The zigzag symbol in figure T-1 is the standard schematic symbol for a resistor, which limits current flow in a circuit.
T6C03: The three-terminal symbol in figure T-1 represents a transistor, identifiable by its base, emitter (with arrow), and collector leads.
T6C04: A circle with an X or filament inside is the standard schematic symbol for a lamp, indicating a component that produces light when current flows.
T6C05: A battery symbol uses alternating long and short parallel lines to represent electrochemical cells providing DC voltage. The long line is positive, the short line is negative.
T6C06: Two parallel lines represent a capacitor's plates separated by a dielectric. Capacitors store energy in an electric field, block DC, and pass AC signals.
T6C07: An LED symbol looks like a standard diode with arrows pointing outward to indicate emitted light. When forward-biased, the semiconductor junction releases photons as visible light.
T6C08: A resistor symbol with an arrow through it indicates adjustable resistance. Moving a wiper contact along the resistive element changes the output value continuously.
T6C09: Two coils drawn side by side represent a transformer's primary and secondary windings. It transfers energy magnetically between circuits, typically changing the voltage level in the process.
T6C10: A coil symbol with an arrow indicates a variable inductor whose inductance can be adjusted, often by sliding a ferromagnetic core in or out. Changing it shifts a circuit's resonant frequency.
T6C11: The antenna symbol represents the element that converts electrical signals into radio waves for transmission or captures incoming waves for the receiver. It is the circuit's interface with free space.
T6C12: Schematics use standardized symbols to accurately show how components connect electrically to one another. Physical size, board layout, and appearance are not represented.
T6D01: A rectifier uses diodes to allow current to pass in only one direction, converting reversing AC into pulsating DC. It is the essential first stage in most power supplies.
T6D02: A relay uses a small current flowing through an electromagnet coil to mechanically move a switch contact. This lets a low-power signal safely control a separate, higher-power circuit.
T6D03: A conductive braid or foil surrounding the inner conductor intercepts stray electromagnetic fields before they couple into or out of the signal wire. This keeps noise out of sensitive signal paths.
T6D04: A meter converts an electrical quantity such as voltage or current into a human-readable number on an analog scale or digital display.
T6D05: A regulator circuit continuously compares output voltage to a reference and corrects deviations, delivering a stable voltage despite input fluctuations or changing load current.
T6D06: A transformer transfers power between two coils through electromagnetic induction; the turns ratio between primary and secondary determines the output voltage. More primary turns than secondary steps voltage down.
T6D07: An LED emits light when forward-biased current passes through its semiconductor junction. LEDs are efficient, long-lived, and available in multiple colors, making them the standard choice for indicators.
T6D08: An inductor and capacitor together resonate at the frequency where their reactances are equal and cancel. This selective LC behavior is the foundation of filters, oscillators, and tuned amplifiers.
T6D09: An integrated circuit combines many transistors, resistors, and other components onto a single silicon chip. This miniaturization delivers complex functions in one compact, inexpensive package.
T6D10: Component 2 in figure T-1 is a transistor, which acts as a controlled valve: a small input signal switches or regulates a much larger current through the output circuit.
T6D11: An LC circuit resonates at the single frequency where inductive and capacitive reactances cancel each other. Series LC passes that frequency; parallel LC rejects it, enabling tuned filters.
T7A01: Sensitivity describes how weak a signal a receiver can reliably detect. A more sensitive receiver can copy faint, distant stations that a less sensitive one would miss entirely.
T7A02: A transceiver combines both a receiver and transmitter into one unit, letting an operator listen and talk without two separate devices.
T7A03: A mixer multiplies two signals together, producing sum and difference frequencies, which shifts a signal from one frequency to another.
T7A04: Selectivity measures how narrowly a receiver can tune to one signal while rejecting adjacent signals crowding the same part of the band.
T7A05: An oscillator uses a feedback loop to sustain a continuous signal at a precise frequency, providing the stable reference a radio needs.
T7A06: A transverter up-converts and down-converts both the transmit and receive paths, letting a radio designed for one band operate on a completely different band.
T7A07: PTT (Push-To-Talk) grounds a control line that switches the radio from receive to transmit mode, typically triggered by pressing a mic button.
T7A08: Modulation impresses audio information onto an RF carrier by varying its amplitude, frequency, or phase so the signal carries voice or data.
T7A09: SSB and FM/CW differ in duty cycle and signal envelope; the switch sets amplifier bias and protection circuits to match each mode's demands.
T7A10: An RF power amplifier boosts the transceiver's low-level output signal to a higher wattage suitable for longer-range transmission.
T7A11: The VFO generates a tunable frequency reference that the transceiver uses to set the exact channel for both receiving and transmitting.
T7B01: Over-deviation means your voice is swinging the FM carrier too wide; backing away from the mic lowers input level and reduces deviation.
T7B02: A consumer receiver with poor front-end selectivity can be overloaded by a nearby strong amateur signal, causing it to receive unintended transmissions.
T7B03: RFI can originate from transmitters, computers, switching power supplies, or poor wiring, so all listed sources are legitimate culprits.
T7B04: High SWR reflects RF power back into the finals; solid-state transceivers detect this and reduce output automatically to protect the transistors.
T7B05: Installing a filter (typically a high-pass or notch filter) at the affected receiver's antenna input blocks the amateur signal before it reaches the front end.
T7B06: Confirming your own TV shows no interference rules out a transmitter fault and suggests the neighbor's equipment lacks adequate filtering or shielding.
T7B07: A band-reject filter notched to the commercial FM band blocks those strong nearby signals from overloading your 2-meter receiver's front end.
T7B08: Proper responses include politely discussing the issue, consulting an ARRL technical advisor, and contacting the FCC if needed — all listed actions are appropriate.
T7B09: Loose or improperly installed coax connectors allow RF to enter the cable system directly; fixing them eliminates the most common ingress point first.
T7B10: Distorted FM audio through a repeater can result from being off-frequency, under- or over-deviation, or a marginal signal — any of these degrade intelligibility.
T7B11: A ferrite choke on the mic cable blocks RF from traveling back into the transmitter's audio input, where it causes distortion.
T7C01: A dummy load absorbs transmitter power as heat instead of radiating it, letting you test equipment without causing on-air interference.
T7C02: An antenna analyzer measures impedance and SWR across a range of frequencies, revealing exactly where the antenna is resonant.
T7C03: The non-inductive resistor presents a pure 50-ohm load with no reactance; the heat sink safely dissipates the absorbed transmitter power.
T7C04: 1:1 means all power transfers to the antenna with nothing reflected back — source and load impedances are perfectly matched.
T7C05: High SWR means reflected power is returning to the amplifier output stage; reducing power prevents that reflected energy from destroying the transistors.
T7C06: SWR of 4:1 means the antenna and feed line impedances don't match, causing significant power to reflect back rather than radiate.
T7C07: Resistance in the feed line's conductors and dielectric converts some signal energy into heat before it ever reaches the antenna.
T7C08: A directional wattmeter measures forward and reflected power separately; SWR is derived from the ratio of those two readings.
T7C09: Water infiltration degrades the dielectric, dramatically increases signal loss, and corrodes both the center conductor and the braid over time.
T7C10: UV radiation breaks down plastic insulation over time, creating cracks that allow moisture inside, raising loss and corroding internal conductors.
T7C11: Air has a lower dielectric constant than solid plastic, so foam-filled coax loses less signal energy per foot of cable.
T7D01: A voltmeter measures the difference in electrical potential between two points; potential is expressed in volts.
T7D02: Connected in parallel across both terminals, the voltmeter reads the potential difference without interrupting or altering current flow through the component.
T7D03: An ammeter must carry all circuit current, so it's inserted in series, breaking the circuit at one point to route current through the meter.
T7D04: An ammeter measures current flow in amperes; its very low internal resistance minimizes its effect on the circuit being tested.
T7D05: The ohmmeter's internal battery supplies a small known current; the meter applies Ohm's law to calculate resistance from the resulting voltage drop.
T7D06: Applying external voltage while set to resistance mode can force current backward through the internal battery circuit, destroying the meter.
T7D07: A multimeter combines voltmeter, ammeter, and ohmmeter functions; voltage and resistance measurement are its two most common uses in electronics work.
T7D08: Acid-core solder is made for plumbing; the corrosive flux residue it leaves behind attacks component leads and PCB traces over time.
T7D09: A cold joint forms when solder does not fully melt or cools too fast, leaving a dull, crystalline, rough surface instead of a smooth shiny finish.
T7D10: The ohmmeter battery begins charging the capacitor, so current flows initially giving low resistance. As the cap charges, current decreases and the meter reads progressively higher resistance.
T7D11: Circuit voltage will damage the ohmmeter and produce false readings. Always power down and discharge capacitors before measuring resistance anywhere in a live circuit.
T8A01: SSB is produced by generating a standard AM signal then filtering out the carrier and one sideband, leaving a single amplitude-modulated sideband carrying the audio.
T8A02: Packet radio sends audio frequency-shift keying tones into a standard FM transceiver, so the transmitted RF signal ends up frequency or phase modulated.
T8A03: SSB puts all transmit power into one narrow 3 kHz sideband with no wasted carrier energy, giving a decisive advantage over FM for pulling in weak distant signals.
T8A04: FM resists amplitude noise well and delivers consistent audio quality, making it the universal choice for local VHF and UHF voice repeater operation.
T8A05: CW is simply a carrier keyed on and off with no audio modulation, requiring only about 150 Hz — far less spectrum than any voice or data mode.
T8A06: Amateur convention sets upper sideband as standard above 10 MHz. Since 10 meters and all VHF/UHF bands fall above that boundary, upper sideband is used.
T8A07: SSB carries only one voice sideband (about 3 kHz) with no carrier, while FM requires 10–15 kHz for its frequency deviation plus guard bands.
T8A08: Human voice spans roughly 300 Hz to 3000 Hz, and SSB transmits exactly that range as a single sideband, making the total bandwidth about 3 kHz.
T8A09: VHF FM voice uses plus-or-minus 5 kHz deviation plus guard bands on each side, putting the total occupied channel width between 10 and 15 kHz.
T8A10: Analog fast-scan TV must carry fine picture detail across hundreds of scan lines plus an audio subcarrier, requiring about 6 MHz — the same as a broadcast TV channel.
T8A11: Morse code needs only enough bandwidth to reproduce the dot-and-dash keying transitions, which amounts to roughly 150 Hz of spectrum.
T8A12: FM capture effect locks the receiver onto the strongest signal and rejects all others, so two simultaneous signals on the same frequency cannot both be received.
T8B01: Beacon transmissions carry onboard sensor readings such as battery voltage and temperatures so ground stations can monitor whether the satellite is healthy and functioning normally.
T8B02: A satellite transponder has limited power; an overpowering uplink consumes a disproportionate share, compressing or blocking weaker signals from other stations sharing the same transponder.
T8B03: Tracking programs use Keplerian orbital elements to compute a satellite real-time azimuth, elevation, and Doppler shift, and to predict upcoming pass windows.
T8B04: Amateur satellites carry linear transponders for SSB and CW contacts, FM transponders for voice access, and digital modes, so all listed transmission types are in use.
T8B05: A satellite beacon is a continuous or periodic transmission from the spacecraft carrying identification and telemetry data so operators can track and monitor its condition.
T8B06: Keplerian elements describe a satellite's orbital parameters—inclination, eccentricity, period, and more. Tracking software uses these values to calculate where the satellite will be at any given time.
T8B07: Like a train whistle sounding higher as it approaches and lower as it departs, a satellite's signal shifts higher in frequency when closing and lower when receding.
T8B08: The letters indicate band: U = UHF (70 cm), V = VHF (2 m). U/V mode means you transmit on 70 cm and receive the satellite's retransmission on 2 m.
T8B09: As the satellite spins, its antenna's polarization rotates relative to your ground antenna, causing the received signal to periodically strengthen and fade.
T8B10: LEO satellites orbit at low altitudes (a few hundred to ~2,000 km), completing a full orbit in roughly 90–100 minutes, making them briefly visible from any ground station.
T8B11: Satellite telemetry is a one-way housekeeping broadcast. Receiving only requires no license, so anyone may listen regardless of amateur status.
T8B12: A linear transponder amplifies all signals in its passband together. Matching your downlink strength to the unmodulated beacon confirms you're neither over-driving nor starving the transponder's shared power budget.
T8C01: Radio direction finding uses a directional antenna to take bearings from multiple locations, then triangulates the precise source of the interference or jamming signal.
T8C02: A directional antenna reveals which bearing produces the strongest signal, letting you systematically home in on the hidden transmitter's location.
T8C03: Contesting is a competitive on-air event where operators race to log as many contacts as possible within a fixed time window, often 24 or 48 hours.
T8C04: Contest efficiency requires sending only your callsign and the required exchange—extra conversation wastes time and airtime for both operators.
T8C05: The Maidenhead system divides the globe into 2°×1° rectangles, each assigned a letter-number code like EN52, widely used in VHF/UHF weak-signal and contest operating.
T8C06: You transmit DTMF touch-tones over the air to the IRLP node's receiver, which decodes them as commands to connect to another node across the internet.
T8C07: VoIP encodes voice as digital packets routed over IP networks—the same technology behind FaceTime and Skype—delivering audio without a traditional phone circuit.
T8C08: IRLP uses VoIP to bridge amateur repeaters and simplex stations over the internet, extending a local radio's reach to nodes anywhere in the world.
T8C09: EchoLink lets a licensed amateur connect to a repeater or another station via the internet from a computer or smartphone, with no local RF transmission required.
T8C10: EchoLink requires call sign registration and proof of license before granting access, ensuring only licensed amateurs can use the system.
T8C11: A gateway station bridges amateur radio and the internet, passing transmissions in both directions between RF and internet-connected systems.
T8D01: PSK31, RTTY, FT8, Winlink, and JS8Call are all digital modes, so every option listed qualifies and all choices are correct.
T8D02: FT8 uses a tightly structured 15-second cycle and advanced error correction to decode signals far below the noise floor, enabling contacts with very weak signals or low power.
T8D03: APRS is a flexible digital protocol that carries position reports, weather data, text messages, and other telemetry — making all listed data types valid payloads.
T8D04: NTSC was the North American analog color television standard, transmitting full-motion video at 30 frames per second using a composite color signal.
T8D05: APRS overlays GPS-derived station positions onto a map display in real time, giving operators shared situational awareness during events or emergencies.
T8D06: PSK encodes digital data by shifting the phase of a carrier wave between defined states rather than varying amplitude or frequency.
T8D07: DMR uses Time Division Multiple Access to split a 12.5 kHz channel into two alternating time slots, doubling capacity without extra spectrum.
T8D08: A packet transmission bundles a source/destination header, the data payload, and a checksum for error detection — all three travel together.
T8D09: CW stands for continuous wave; the transmitter's unmodulated carrier is switched on and off in Morse code patterns to convey characters.
T8D10: WSJT-X bundles modes like FT8, FT4, WSPR, and MSK144, supporting weak-signal HF contacts, meteor scatter, EME, and beacon monitoring.
T8D11: ARQ has the receiver check each block for errors; if one is found, it sends a retransmit request so the sender resends that block.
T8D12: Amateur mesh networks like AREDN repurpose 802.11 Wi-Fi hardware with custom firmware to create self-healing, multi-hop amateur data networks.
T9A01: A beam antenna uses directors and reflectors to focus radiated energy in one direction, increasing gain toward the target at the expense of other directions.
T9A02: When a physical antenna is too short, adding a series inductor (loading coil) increases its electrical length to reach resonance.
T9A03: Polarization describes which way the electric field oscillates; a vertical element produces vertical polarization, a horizontal one produces horizontal polarization.
T9A04: The stubby rubber-duck antenna is far shorter than a quarter wave, so it radiates inefficiently and much of the transmitter power is wasted as heat.
T9A05: A dipole's resonant frequency is inversely proportional to its length; trimming the elements raises the frequency at which it naturally resonates.
T9A06: A Yagi uses parasitic director and reflector elements to focus energy in one direction, producing substantially more gain than a simple dipole or vertical.
T9A07: A car's metal body acts as a partial Faraday cage, blocking and absorbing RF, so an interior antenna suffers significant signal loss versus an external mount.
T9A08: On the 2-meter band (~146 MHz) a quarter wavelength works out to about 19 inches, making that length naturally resonant with low feedpoint impedance.
T9A09: The 5/8-wave whip has a lower radiation angle than a quarter wave, directing more energy toward the horizon where other stations are, yielding roughly 3 dB more gain.
T9A10: A dipole radiates most strongly at right angles (broadside) to its length because current flow is greatest at the center and the fields add constructively in that direction.
T9A11: Antennas dont create power; gain describes how effectively one focuses energy in a chosen direction compared to a reference antenna like an isotropic radiator. More gain in one direction means less in others.
T9B01: Moisture intrusion corrodes connector pins and the center conductor, degrading signal and raising SWR. PL-259s, N-types, and BNC connectors all benefit from weatherproofing tape when installed outdoors.
T9B02: 50 ohms is an engineering compromise between minimum loss (around 77 ohms in air) and maximum power handling (around 30 ohms), making it ideal for amateur transmit-and-receive use.
T9B03: Coax is shielded, so it doesnt radiate or pick up interference, and it can be routed near metal or through walls without special spacing requirements, simplifying installation.
T9B04: Maximum power transfers when source and load impedances match. The tuner adjusts the impedance seen by the transceiver to its design value (typically 50 ohms), minimizing reflected power.
T9B05: Higher frequencies increase skin-effect losses in the conductors and dielectric losses in the insulation, so a given length of coax attenuates a signal more at 440 MHz than at 144 MHz.
T9B06: Type N connectors have a precision threaded interface and geometry designed to maintain constant impedance at microwave frequencies, unlike PL-259s which degrade significantly above a few hundred MHz.
T9B07: PL-259s (often called UHF connectors despite the misleading name) are robust and widely used through HF and VHF, but their large, uncontrolled geometry causes losses above roughly 300 MHz.
T9B08: Coax loss comes from conductor resistance, dielectric absorption in the insulation, and radiation from damaged or wet sections. All three mechanisms waste signal power as heat.
T9B09: A loose or corroded connection changes its contact resistance intermittently, altering the impedance the transmitter sees and causing the SWR reading to jump around unpredictably.
T9B10: RG-213 uses a larger center conductor and better dielectric than RG-58, reducing both resistive and dielectric loss per unit length, especially noticeable at VHF and above.
T9B11: Air has lower dielectric loss than any solid plastic, and hardline uses a rigid outer conductor with a large diameter, combining both advantages for the lowest possible feed-line loss.
T9B12: SWR compares the amplitude of forward and reflected waves on a feed line. A perfect 1:1 match means no reflections; higher ratios indicate impedance mismatch and wasted power.
T0A01: Even at only 12 volts, a large battery can deliver hundreds of amps into a short circuit, instantly vaporizing metal and igniting nearby material or igniting hydrogen gas from the cells.
T0A02: Current through the body can cause ventricular fibrillation, severe burns at entry and exit points, and involuntary muscle contractions that prevent letting go of the source.
T0A03: US electrical code assigns black insulation to the hot (ungrounded) conductor, which carries the line voltage and is the one that can shock you if touched.
T0A04: A fuse contains a wire sized to melt at its rated current, opening the circuit before excess current can overheat wiring, damage equipment, or start a fire.
T0A05: A fuse protects the wiring, not just the device. Replacing a 5 A fuse with a 20 A fuse allows four times the design current to flow, potentially igniting insulation before the fuse opens.
T0A06: Proper grounding, using a safety interlock, and never working alone all address different shock pathways. Combining all three gives the best protection at a station.
T0A07: Mounting the arrester on a grounded panel at the building entry diverts lightning surge current to earth before it can travel down the feed line into the shack and damage equipment.
T0A08: A fuse interrupts fault current by opening the hot (energized) conductor; placing it on the neutral would leave equipment at full voltage even after the fuse blows, creating a shock hazard.
T0A09: Multiple separate ground points can sit at different potentials during a lightning strike; bonding them together equalizes voltage and creates a single low-impedance path to earth.
T0A10: Rapid charge or discharge drives high current through internal resistance, generating heat; this can cause electrolyte to boil and vent flammable or toxic gases.
T0A11: Large filter capacitors store charge at high voltage and discharge slowly; touching internal leads immediately after shutdown can deliver a potentially lethal shock.
T0A12: Leads and meter rated below the measured voltage can arc or have insulation fail, exposing the user to shock or starting a fire.
T0B01: Lightning energy is essentially RF; long runs and sharp bends add inductance that impedes the fast-rising surge, so short straight connections carry the energy to ground most efficiently.
T0B02: Safe tower climbing requires a full-body harness, a trained helper or observer on the ground, and knowledge of fall-arrest techniques — all three together.
T0B03: If a lone climber becomes injured or stuck, no one is present to summon help or perform a rescue; a ground observer is always required.
T0B04: A falling tower or antenna can easily contact overhead power lines, creating an electrocution hazard for anyone on or near the structure.
T0B05: Vibration from wind causes turnbuckles to rotate and back off over time; a safety wire locked through the barrel prevents unwinding and loss of guy tension.
T0B06: A ten-foot buffer ensures that even if the antenna collapses completely, it cannot bridge the gap to energized power conductors and create an electrocution risk.
T0B07: Crank-up sections rely on cable tension; without retraction or mechanical locks, the nested sections can drop under a climber's weight, causing a fatal fall.
T0B08: Individual rods at each leg provide multiple low-resistance earth contacts, and bonding them together prevents dangerous potential differences between legs during a lightning event.
T0B09: Utility poles often carry high-voltage distribution lines; an antenna mounted there could contact those wires if it shifts, sags, or falls.
T0B10: Bends create inductance that chokes the steeply rising current wavefront of a lightning strike, diverting energy away from the intended ground path.
T0B11: Part 97 does not specify tower grounding details; the National Electrical Code and applicable local codes set the binding requirements for ground rod depth, wire size, and bonding.
T0C01: Radio waves are electromagnetic radiation with photon energies far too low to knock electrons free from atoms, so they are classified as non-ionizing, unlike X-rays or gamma rays.
T0C02: At 50 MHz the human body is near whole-body resonant frequency and absorbs RF most efficiently, so the FCC sets the tightest maximum permissible exposure limit there.
T0C03: MPE limits are based on time-averaged power; halving the duty cycle halves average exposure, so the allowable instantaneous power density can double while staying within the same average limit.
T0C04: RF exposure depends on transmitter power, antenna gain, operating frequency, distance to the antenna, and the fraction of time transmitting — all of these interact to determine actual dose.
T0C05: Biological tissue absorbs RF energy most efficiently at certain frequencies due to resonance effects in the body, so the threshold for harmful heating differs across the spectrum.
T0C06: Calculation using published formulas, direct measurement with calibrated equipment, and professional assessment are all recognized methods — any one of them satisfies the FCC evaluation requirement.
T0C07: RF current passing through skin generates heat in the tissue, producing a burn similar to a thermal burn but caused by absorbed electromagnetic energy.
T0C08: RF field strength drops sharply with distance, so moving antennas farther from people is one of the most effective ways to reduce exposure.
T0C09: Changing power level, antenna type, feed line, or operating frequency all alter your RF footprint, so each modification triggers a new compliance evaluation under Part 97.
T0C10: Safety limits are based on average power absorbed over time, not peak power alone, so a transmitter that is on only part of the time poses less cumulative risk.
T0C11: Duty cycle is simply the fraction of the averaging period during which the transmitter is actually on, expressed as a percentage.
T0C12: RF photons carry far too little energy to break chemical bonds or damage DNA; they can only deposit heat in tissue, unlike X-rays or gamma rays.
T0C13: Part 97 places the obligation on the station licensee to ensure that no person — including the public — is exposed to RF levels exceeding FCC limits.
